description: Table 2 is a text-only comparison table (no micrographs, plots, axes or scale bars): six rows of tensile data for Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels. Column headers as printed: "Fe–Mn–Al–C steel (wt.%)", "Ultimate strength (MPa)", "Yield strength (MPa)", "Phase", "Ultimate elongation (%)" and "Product of strength and ductility (GPa %)". Rows in reading order, given as ultimate strength / yield strength / phase / ultimate elongation / product: Fe–28Mn–10Al–1.0C [50] — 873 / 572 / γ / 98.9 / 86; Fe–20Mn–9Al–0.6C [23] — 830 / 535 / γ + α (34%) / 45.6 / 38; Fe–18Mn–10Al–1.2C [26] — 875 / 702 / γ + κ / 77.4 / 68; Fe–18Mn–10Al–0.8C [26] — 966 / 801 / γ + κ + α (24%) / 44 / 43; Fe–12Mn–8.0Al–0.8C [27] — 920 / 670 / γ + κ + α (21%) / 46.4 / 43; Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C (present steel) — 855 / 651 / γ + α (40%) + boundary κ / 36.6 / 31. Bracketed numbers are literature references. The table shows the present steel has the lowest elongation and lowest strength–ductility product of the set, and that the α-containing steels have lower elongations than the α-free γ and γ + κ steels.

observations.observation: The table contains exactly six data rows and five property/identity columns: Fe–Mn–Al–C steel (wt.%), Ultimate strength (MPa), Yield strength (MPa), Phase, Ultimate elongation (%), Product of strength and ductility (GPa %).

The present-steel row reads: Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C (present steel), ultimate strength 855 MPa, yield strength 651 MPa, phase γ + α (40%) + boundary κ, ultimate elongation 36.6%, product of strength and ductility 31 GPa%.
Highest ultimate strength in the table is 966 MPa (Fe–18Mn–10Al–0.8C) and highest ultimate elongation is 98.9% (Fe–28Mn–10Al–1.0C).
The highest product of strength and ductility printed is 86 GPa% for Fe–28Mn–10Al–1.0C and the lowest is 31 GPa% for Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C (present steel).

α-phase fractions are printed in parentheses in the Phase column: (34%) for Fe–20Mn–9Al–0.6C, (24%) for Fe–18Mn–10Al–0.8C, (21%) for Fe–12Mn–8.0Al–0.8C and (40%) for the present steel; the two γ-bearing comparison steels list no α fraction.

The caption states the table lists ultimate strength, yield strength, ultimate elongation and the product of strength and ductility of several Fe–Mn–Al–C steels; the caption prints the phrase 'product of strength of strength and ductility'.

The citing text states the present steel gives ultimate strength 855 MPa, yield strength 651 MPa, ultimate elongation 36.6% and product of strength and ductility 31 GPa% after annealing at 900 °C for 1 h.

The citing text states the ultimate elongation of the present steel is the lowest among the steels in Table 2, attributed to the highest α phase fraction, boundary κ-carbide between large α grains and an inhomogeneous microstructure.

The citing text states that steels containing α phase (Fe–20Mn–9Al–0.6C, Fe–18Mn–10Al–0.8C, Fe–12Mn–8.0Al–0.8C) have lower ultimate elongations than steels containing no α phase (Fe–28Mn–10Al–1.0C, Fe–18Mn–10Al–1.2C).

The citing text states that κ-carbide dispersed in the austenite matrix of Fe–18Mn–10Al–1.2C, Fe–18Mn–10Al–0.8C and Fe–12Mn–8.0Al–0.8C promotes planar glide during deformation and contributes to strength.
Reference-number mismatch between table and text: the table labels Fe–20Mn–9Al–0.6C as [23], whereas the citing text refers to this steel as [25] and describes the literature set as [25–27,50].

The table itself contains no images, curves or statistical graphics — it is a pure tabulation of literature and present-steel tensile data, so it supports no visual trend other than the printed numbers.

subfigures.description: Single-panel data table listing six Fe–Mn–Al–C steels (five from literature [50], [23], [26], [26], [27] plus the present steel) with ultimate strength (MPa), yield strength (MPa), phase constitution, ultimate elongation (%) and product of strength and ductility (GPa %). All cells are legible; no graphic panels, axes or scale bars are present.
